verses.text: In the twenty-third year of Joash the son of Ahaziah, king of Judah, Jehoahaz the son of Jehu began to reign over Israel in Samaria for seventeen years.
He did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight, and followed the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, with which he made Israel to sin. He didn’t depart from it.
Yahweh’s anger burned against Israel, and he delivered them into the hand of Hazael king of Syria, and into the hand of Benhadad the son of Hazael, continually.
Jehoahaz begged Yahweh, and Yahweh listened to him; for he saw the oppression of Israel, how the king of Syria oppressed them.
(Yahweh gave Israel a savior, so that they went out from under the hand of the Syrians; and the children of Israel lived in their tents as before.
Nevertheless they didn’t depart from the sins of the house of Jeroboam, with which he made Israel to sin, but walked in them; and the Asherah also remained in Samaria.)
For he didn’t leave to Jehoahaz of the people any more than fifty horsemen, and ten chariots, and ten thousand footmen; for the king of Syria destroyed them, and made them like the dust in threshing.
Now the rest of the acts of Jehoahaz, and all that he did, and his might, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
Jehoahaz slept with his fathers; and they buried him in Samaria; and Joash his son reigned in his place.
In the thirty-seventh year of Joash king of Judah, Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz began to reign over Israel in Samaria for sixteen years.
He did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight. He didn’t depart from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, with which he made Israel to sin; but he walked in them.
Now the rest of the acts of Joash, and all that he did, and his might with which he fought against Amaziah king of Judah, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
Joash slept with his fathers; and Jeroboam sat on his throne. Joash was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel.
Now Elisha became sick with the illness of which he died; and Joash the king of Israel came down to him, and wept over him, and said, “My father, my father, the chariots of Israel and its horsemen!”
Elisha said to him, “Take bow and arrows”; and he took bow and arrows for himself.
He said to the king of Israel, “Put your hand on the bow”; and he put his hand on it. Elisha laid his hands on the king’s hands.

He said, “Open the window eastward”; and he opened it. Then Elisha said, “Shoot!” and he shot. He said, “Yahweh’s arrow of victory, even the arrow of victory over Syria; for you will strike the Syrians in Aphek, until you have consumed them.”
He said, “Take the arrows”; and he took them. He said to the king of Israel, “Strike the ground”; and he struck three times, and stopped.

The man of God was angry with him, and said, “You should have struck five or six times. Then you would have struck Syria until you had consumed it; whereas now you will strike Syria just three times.”
Elisha died, and they buried him. Now the bands of the Moabites invaded the land at the coming in of the year.
As they were burying a man, behold, they saw a band of raiders; and they threw the man into Elisha’s tomb. As soon as the man touched Elisha’s bones, he revived, and stood up on his feet.
Hazael king of Syria oppressed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz.

But Yahweh was gracious to them, and had compassion on them, and had respect for them, because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and would not destroy them, and he didn’t cast them from his presence as yet.
Hazael king of Syria died; and Benhadad his son reigned in his place.

Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz took again out of the hand of Benhadad the son of Hazael the cities which he had taken out of the hand of Jehoahaz his father by war. Joash struck him three times, and recovered the cities of Israel.

footnotes.content: Jehoahaz begins his reign in dark times—seventeen years ahead of him while his kingdom crumbles under enemy weight. It strikes me how the Lord places leaders not in moments of triumph, but in the valley, where all their strength will show as weakness without Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He walks in the old sin, the pattern set by Jeroboam—and yet these are his choices, made freely, even knowingly. How often I've seen people cling to what destroys them, refusing the turn that would save.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord's anger burns, not in spite, but as a Father who removes what props us up when we've turned away. Syria's grip tightens—a mercy wrapped in pain, meant to drive him back home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At last he begs. Not in strength or negotiation, but in desperation—and the Lord listens. There's something holy about a man finally broken enough to cry out. The Lord sees the oppression, yes, but He also sees the breaking heart that opens to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A savior rises—not a king Jehoahaz can see or touch, but a deliverance the Lord gives because He keeps covenant. How tenderly the Lord provides escape routes for those who call on Him, even when they don't deserve it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Delivered from the Syrians, yet the sin remains—the Asherah pole still stands in Samaria. There's a sobering truth here: the Lord can rescue us from our enemies while we hold fast to what ruins us from within.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fifty horsemen left—that's all. The Syrian king has ground Israel's army to dust. When we see how few survive, we understand what salvation truly means: not restoration to strength, but rescue itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His deeds are recorded in the books of the chronicles—as they are recorded in the mind of God. Even kings whose names fade from common memory are known completely by Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehoahaz sleeps, buried in Samaria—his kingdom passed to his son. He lived through oppression and deliverance, but left his son the same broken inheritance. A king's legacy is often the road he walks, for good or ill.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehoash—same father's legacy, same name nearly, a new reign. Sixteen years ahead of him. Will he choose differently? The text already answers: no. But each soul must still choose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He walks in the sins of Jeroboam—knowing the path, yet choosing it. There's a hardness in that "didn't depart." Sometimes the greatest tragedy is a heart that refuses to turn, even when the way home stands open.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His might is written down—his wars, his struggles against Judah. But here's a whisper I hear: what is might without wisdom? What is victory without the Lord's blessing? The chronicles record only dust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehoash sleeps with his fathers, and Jeroboam takes the throne—another name, another reign, but the same old idolatry carries on. Kings fall, the kingdom staggers, but God's patience remains.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elisha lies dying—the man who walked with Elijah, who parted the Jordan, now fading. Yet the king comes to him weeping, calling him "father." There's a tenderness in that cry: even a king knows some men are worth more than thrones.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Take bow and arrows, Elisha says—simple things, common tools. In the prophet's hands they become instruments of God's purpose. The Lord uses what's at hand when a soul is ready to listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elisha lays his hands on the king's hands—an old man's hands upon a young man's, transferring a blessing. There's power in that touch, not by magic, but by faith. The prophet joins his might to the king's need.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Open the window—let the arrow fly toward Aphek, toward Syria, toward deliverance. "Yahweh's arrow of victory"—what the king shoots is made holy by the Lord's covenant, not the king's aim. Readers today hear an echo of how the Lord arms those who trust Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Take the arrows again—now not toward the window, but to the ground. Simple strikes, repeated actions, a test of obedience and faith. The king must act; his action will measure his trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three times he struck, and stopped—and the prophet grieves. "You should have struck five or six times." The king's hesitation, his half-measure, limits his own victory. How often do we settle for less because we lack the courage to follow through?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elisha dies and is buried—his earthly work is done. But the Lord's work doesn't end with a prophet's death. The bands of Moabites come, the struggle continues, and yet something of Elisha's faith lingers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A man touches Elisha's bones and revives—one final sign that the Lord's power belongs to Him alone, not confined to the living, not bound by death. It's a strange grace, pointing toward a greater resurrection yet to come.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hazael oppressed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz—the weight of an enemy king, pressing down year after year. Oppression is patient; it waits. But the Lord's mercy waits longer still.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yet the Lord was gracious—because of His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, He doesn't destroy them or cast them away. That ancient promise holds; it's the anchor that keeps Israel from drowning, the thread that ties all generations together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hazael dies; his son Benhadad reigns. One oppressor falls, another rises—the cycle of earthly power. But the Lord remains; His covenant outlasts any king.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehoash recovers the cities—three victories, mirroring the three strikes of the arrows. Limited as they were, they bore fruit. The king's hesitation cost him more, but mercy still came. Sometimes we don't get all we could have had, yet what we do receive is enough to turn the tide.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
